newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia govt campaigns in Kosovo, promises aid.
newsitem.headline: Serbia govt campaigns in Kosovo, promises aid.

text.p: Serbia's government on Thursday met in the capital of its troubled Kosovo province, reasserting its authority and promising economic help for the powderkeg region where ethnic Serbs are outnumbered nine to one by Albanians.

The government session, held with an eye to Serbia's September presidential and parliamentary elections, discussed regional development strategy, opened a new regional development office in the capital Pristina and promised more state aid to the economically backward region.
"The fact that the office is based in this part of the republic shows our readiness to work rapidly on the development of the province," Marjanovic said after the session.
"Kosovo, as an integral part of Serbia constitutionally and politically, must be an economically integrated part of the republic," Marjanovic said.
Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians are effectively deprived of any political voice, is widely regarded as a powder keg which, if ignited, could wreck international peace efforts in the Balkans.
The session in Pristina, chaired by Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic and held behind closed doors, is the first Serbian government session in the province for at least a decade.
Marjanovic insisted that the government's reforms aimed to encompass all segments of society and treat Serbia as a whole.

"Proof of this is the government's presence in Pristina to set up the regional development office. This institution is an instrument of support for speedy development of less developed areas in Serbia... and funds will be provided by the budget," the Prime Minister said.

Under the new electoral law, Kosovo provides 42 seats for the 250-seat Serbian parliament and the ruling Socialists are heavily counting on those since ethnic Albanians have vowed to boycott the elections on September 21.
Pristina's Albanian language media did not expect Serbian ministers to meet ethnic Albanian politicians and party leaders in Kosovo.

The United States has made an improvement in Serbia's treatment of Kosovo one of its conditions for lifting remaining sanctions in force against federal Yugoslavia, which consists of Serbia and the tiny republic of Montenegro.

Speaking in a province where support for close ties or outright union with neighbouring Albania is strong, Marjanovic reaffirmed that Kosovo would remain part of Serbia, saying there was no basis for militant separatism and no reason for ethnic Albanians to want to leave.
"We shall energetically stand up against all attempts at confrontation, terror and different projects of division and dividing maps. Kosovo is part of Serbia and Yugoslavia...," Marjanovic said.
Marjanovic urged ethnic Albanians to exercise their rights which he said was the only way to shift them away from "the economic, political, social and civilisational margins".
Serbia revoked Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, claiming its Albanian population wanted to secede and join neighbouring Albania.
The Albanians have boycotted Serbian institutions since, and their leaders have openly called for secession, forcing the U.S. to warn them this was not an option and to find a solution within Serbia.
All Serb-Albanian talks over the past few months to find a solution to the impasse have been deadlocked.
In the meantime the province has been rocked over the past year by a wave of violence in which more than 30 people have been killed, despite a heavy Serbian police and army presence.
Clandestine Albanian organisations have been blamed for the attacks and scores of ethnic Albanians have been sentenced to stiff prison sentences.
The ruling Serbian Socialists' election campaign promises include reforms and economic development of the country, now emerging from under U.N. sanctions for its involvement in the war in Bosnia.
